newsitem.title: UK: Queen's press chief resigns, new man is Australian.
newsitem.headline: Queen's press chief resigns, new man is Australian.

text.p: Queen Elizabeth's press chief is resigning his post after six turbulent years for the monarchy and will be replaced by an Australian who used to work for Princess Diana.

Buckingham Palace said on Monday that Charles Anson, 52, who put over the royal family's views on the acrimonious break-up of Diana's marriage to heir-to-the-throne Prince Charles, will join Grand Met, one of Britain's leading food and drinks conglomerates, in February 1997.
Anson's move back into industry was expected and he will be replaced by the queen's current deputy press secretary, Geoffrey Crawford.

Crawford, a 46-year-old Australian, resigned as Diana's aide a year ago because she failed to tell him of her decision to give a full and frank television interview in which she discussed her marriage, her adultery and her views on Charles's suitability as a king.
"It has been a great honour to work for the queen and the Duke of Edinburgh and their family, and I thoroughly enjoyed these six years," Anson told reporters.
Anson took up his post in 1990 as it became clear to the press and public that the fairytale marriage of Charles and Diana had turned sour.

He was at the palace for what the queen termed her "annus horribilis" (horrible year) in 1992. That was when Charles and Diana separated and the marriage of Prince Andrew, the queen's second son, and his wife Sarah "Fergie" Ferguson collapsed.
Anson played a large part in the decision to open up royal finances to more public scrutiny and the queen's move to start paying income tax.

He has battled to preserve the reputation of the monarchy at a time when respect for the royal family has plummeted and former colonies such as Australia and Canada have discussed the possibility of becoming republics.
Buckingham Palace said Crawford will hold his new post for three years and then return to Australia.
He is well-liked among journalists and valued by the royal family for his down-to-earth advice.

Crawford is well-used to handling delicate situations, having looked after Diana's interests after her separation from Charles and represented Fergie during her brief period as a member of the royal family.
Royal writer Margaret Holden said of him once: "He is straightforward, unstuffy and seems to have bags of that vital ingredient, common sense."
